title: EU AI Act Article 14: What Human Oversight Does High-Risk AI Require?
context: 2026-08-27 — Article 14 is a standing duty for every high-risk AI system, and the compliance gap most often cited in early audits as deployers prepare for the Annex III high-risk classification window.
body: Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons for the period the system is in use. The purpose is not to rubber-stamp automated decisions but to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights. Oversight takes two recognised forms: human-in-the-loop, where a person can intervene in each individual decision cycle, and human-on-the-loop, where a person can monitor the system and stop or override it. Two specific capabilities are mandated. First, operators must be able to properly understand the system's capacities and limitations, so they are not misled by automation bias. Second, operators must be able to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the system or to disregard, override, or reverse its output. Oversight must be proportionate to the risk and the level of autonomy of the system, and it must be borne by a natural person — an organisation cannot discharge Article 14 by pointing to a purely automated control. The practical test the Council of AI applies is whether an operator can answer, for a concrete decision, three questions: what did the system do, why, and what could I have done instead — and whether that answer is backed by an auditable record. Monitoring an oversight control is monitored containment rather than provable isolation: you cannot prove no failure will ever pass a human reviewer, but you can keep a signed measurement of what the reviewer saw and did, carried in a verified measurement credential. For deployers approaching the high-risk classification window, Article 14 is worth instrumenting early, because retrofitting human oversight onto a system already in production is the single most expensive compliance correction.
